hook.title: Painting one stroke at a time
hook.text: You want a machine that paints digits. A 28×28 picture has 784 pixels, far too many to describe at once. So paint like a person does: start top-left, and choose each pixel *after looking at everything already painted*. The first stroke needs no context; the second considers the first; the 784th considers the previous 783. Multiply the probabilities of all those choices and you have the probability of the whole picture. That's the **chain rule**, and it's always legal.
hook.recall: Remember the painter: every pixel is chosen after looking at the earlier strokes. Probability of the picture = product of the stroke probabilities, and sampling must go stroke by stroke.

explore.intro: A 3-pixel FVSBN: $\hat x_i=\sigma(\alpha_0^i+\sum_{j<i}\alpha_j^ix_j)$. Toggle pixels and move weights.
tasks: Choose $x=(0,1,1)$. Read off the three factors and check that their product equals the table entry.
Press **Sample** repeatedly. In which order are pixels decided?
explore.takeaway: $p(x_1,x_2,x_3)=p(x_1)\,p(x_2|x_1)\,p(x_3|x_1,x_2)$. Evaluate by multiplying conditionals; sample by drawing one pixel at a time. The 8 probabilities always sum to 1.

build.prompt: Order the steps to **sample** an image from an autoregressive model (FVSBN).
items: Sample $\bar x_3\sim p(x_3\mid x_1=\bar x_1,x_2=\bar x_2)$
build.explanation: Slide 6 lists this exact sequence. Each pixel conditions on the samples already drawn, so generation cannot be parallelised.

questions.explanation: Multiply the three conditionals: $(1-0.8)\times0.3\times0.6=0.2\times0.18=0.036$, as in the slide's $(1-\hat x_1)\hat x_2\hat x_3$ example.

questions.prompt: Which factorisation of $p(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ is the autoregressive chain rule?
questions.explanation: Each variable conditions on **all earlier ones** in the chosen ordering, the painter looking at earlier strokes.

questions.prompt: How many parameters does an FVSBN over $n=10$ pixels have (sum of the sizes of all logistic regressions, including biases)? Slide: $1+2+3+\dots+n$.
Which statement about FVSBN is FALSE?
options: Each conditional $p(x_i|x_{<i})$ is Bernoulli with a logistic-regression parameter
To evaluate $p(x)$ you multiply all the conditionals
You can sample all pixels in parallel because each conditional is independent of the others
questions.explanation: Conditionals depend on earlier pixels, so the painter must decide pixel $i$ before pixel $i+1$. Sampling is sequential.

questions.prompt: A student says: *“To sample from my autoregressive model I draw every pixel independently from its marginal $p(x_i)$.”* What’s wrong?
options: The conditional $p(x_i\mid x_{<i})$ must be used with the *already-sampled* earlier pixels. Marginals ignore the dependencies the chain rule encodes
Pixels should be sampled right to left
questions.explanation: The painter looks back at earlier strokes. Independent marginal sampling would give noise, not digits.

questions.prompt: Why are the conditionals $p(x_i\mid x_{<i})$ parameterised by logistic regressions rather than stored as tables?
options: The conditionals are too complex to store in tabular form (the table size explodes)
questions.explanation: A table for $p(x_{784}|x_1..x_{783})$ would need $2^{783}$ rows; a logistic regression compresses it to 784 numbers.
